title: Grant peace
hook: the Amidah ends asking for peace, goodness and blessing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Modim, the thanks no one can say for you. Your line was we thank you. Did you thank someone yourself? Today, the last blessing of the Amidah. Day five hundred ninety-four.

Think of how many things end on peace. Shalom is the word for hello and for goodbye. The Kaddish ends on it. So does the priestly blessing from the book of Numbers. Even the Mishnah, the great code of Jewish law, sixty-three tractates of rules about fields, festivals, courts and purity, closes its very last page with a sentence about peace. The Amidah follows the same pattern. After praise, after thirteen requests, after thanks, the very last thing it asks for is shalom.
screen: `HELLO, GOODBYE: SHALOM.` → `THE MISHNAH'S LAST PAGE.` → `THE AMIDAH'S LAST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: In the leader's morning repetition, just before this blessing, comes the priestly blessing. In the old Jewish translation, it ends: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." In Israel, descendants of the priests, kohanim, come forward and say it every day; in many communities outside Israel, they do so on festivals. Then the last blessing picks up the thread: Sim shalom. Grant peace, goodness and blessing, grace, kindness and compassion, to us and to all Your people Israel. Bless us, our Father, all of us as one, with the light of Your face. Blessed are You, who blesses Your people Israel with peace. The light of Your face is borrowed straight from the priestly blessing before it. All of us as one: peace is something no one can have alone. Shalom comes from a root meaning whole, complete. It's not only the absence of fighting. It's nothing missing. In many Ashkenazi communities, the afternoon and evening services use a shorter version, Shalom Rav, abundant peace. And that sentence on the Mishnah's last page? Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta says that God found no vessel that could hold blessing except peace, and quotes the Psalm: "the LORD will bless His people with peace." A vessel: all the other blessings, health, livelihood, wisdom, leak out without it. So the Amidah puts the container last, to hold everything that came before.
screen: `THE PRIESTLY BLESSING: GIVE THEE PEACE.` · `ALL OF US AS ONE.` · `SHALOM: WHOLE, NOTHING MISSING.` · `THE ONLY VESSEL THAT HOLDS BLESSING.` · then, large: `GRANT PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish peace on one person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose life feels un-whole right now: someone grieving, someone in a fight, someone pulled in too many directions. Picture them clearly. On each out-breath, send them one piece of what's missing: rest, calm, a quiet evening, a phone call that goes well. If you pray, you can ask for their shalom. If it's someone you're in conflict with, notice whether you can wish it for them too. The bell holds the time.
Sim Shalom. Grant peace. The Amidah's final blessing: peace, goodness and blessing, for all of us as one.
Your line: grant peace. Today, do one thing that makes something in someone's life more whole: finish what you promised, fix what you broke, or simply show up. Day five hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Sim Shalom is the final blessing of the Amidah, following the priestly blessing in the morning repetition; many Ashkenazi communities say the shorter Shalom Rav at the afternoon and evening services.

original.note: Hebrew: grant peace. shalom from sh-l-m, whole, complete.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice wish for peace at the end.
what it means: the container for every other blessing: wholeness, for all of us as one.
what a scholar hears: Numbers 6:24–26 precedes it in the repetition; Mishnah Uktzin 3:12 quotes Psalm 29:11; Shalom Rav in the Ashkenazi afternoon and evening rite.

notes: Numbers 6:26 and Psalm 29:11 quoted as JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Shalom Rav at Mincha and Maariv in Ashkenazi rite (Sim Shalom at Mincha on fast days); confirm.
